tagline: Catalog user-owned samples, preview them in key and tempo, and organize collections

tiers.name: Creator
tiers.notes: Live promotion advertises $4.99 for the first month; standard recurring price is recorded.

tiers.name: INSTRUMENT
tiers.limits: Unlimited premium presets; 0 sample credits included.

tiers.name: Splice x Ableton Live
tiers.limits: Up to 100 samples/day inside Ableton Live; 100 one-time introductory credits after trial; requires Live 12.3+.

pricing.freeTierCaps: Browse and preview the catalog and claim selected free drops; no numeric free-download cap is publicly stated.
pricing.billingTerms: Monthly only; no annual Sounds subscription was publicly offered.
pricing.hiddenCosts: Samples generally cost 1 credit while presets/MIDI can cost up to 3; unused credits roll only while active and expire 28 days after the final billing period; a subscription can be paused for up to 2 months; rent-to-own plugins are separate purchases.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Splice, catalog user-owned samples, preview them in key and tempo, and organize collections. The hard boundary is licensed sample catalog, creator network, desktop sync, rights clarity, and discovery, plus licensed content, rights, and distribution network.
coreLoopDIY: Catalog user-owned samples, analyze local files to preview them in key and tempo, and organize collections for a private production workflow.
whatYouLose: licensed sample catalog, creator network, desktop sync, rights clarity, and discovery
moatNotes: licensed content, rights, and distribution network
ongoingBurden: catalog licensing, royalties, identity, content delivery, moderation, recommendations, payouts, codecs, and rights disputes
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Splice because the product is the catalog, rights chain, and distribution network; a player or processing tool is only the visible edge. The recurring cost buys catalog licensing, royalties, identity, content delivery, moderation, recommendations, payouts, codecs, and rights disputes, not just the visible interface.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Sounds Plus plan and a personal library or creator utility DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Splice in an empty repository.
Use Python 3.12, FastAPI, SQLite, ffmpeg, and a local web interface; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: catalog user-owned samples, analyze local files to preview them in key and tempo, and organize collections for a private production workflow.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Index only user-selected folders and preserve source audio without modification.
Read tags and artwork, calculate loudness and waveform data, and detect exact duplicates by hash.
Provide albums, artists, playlists, search, queue, favorites, and resumable local playback.
Add optional creator tools for trim, normalize, split stems through a local model, and export new files.
Keep all rights and source information attached to imported tracks and display it during export.
Document that the application does not provide music, licensing, distribution, or royalty collection.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out copyrighted catalog acquisition or sharing.
Deliberately leave out streaming-service circumvention.
Deliberately leave out royalty accounting, label distribution, and global content delivery.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
